title: The Sentence Nobody Corrected Becomes the Success Metric
description: An unrealistic expectation stated in a kickoff meeting and left unaddressed doesn't go away — it quietly becomes the standard the whole engagement gets judged against.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when a client statement sets an unscoped, unverified success metric for an engagement
Distinguish what's knowable at kickoff from what isn't, and communicate that distinction to a non-technical client

contentSections.body: In a kickoff call, a client says, 'Once this AI system is live, we're planning to let go of three of our five data-entry staff next quarter.' You haven't scoped the project yet. You don't know if the system can handle the edge cases those three people currently catch, or how long it'll take to reach a reliable accuracy rate on this client's specific data. Saying nothing and moving on to the technical agenda means this exact sentence becomes the client's success metric — and if reality doesn't match it in three months, the project reads as a failure regardless of what the technology actually achieved.

The specific consulting skill here isn't technical — it's naming the expectation gap out loud, in the room, before it becomes silent scope. That means separating what's actually knowable at kickoff (this system can plausibly handle routine cases based on early testing) from what isn't (a specific headcount and a specific date), and being explicit that a headcount decision shouldn't be made on a pre-scoping guess.

Avoiding this conversation because it's uncomfortable is exactly how 'we brought in an AI consultant and it didn't deliver' narratives start. Usually the technology performed reasonably — the actual failure was an expectation nobody corrected early enough, which then hardened into the standard everyone judged the project against.

contentSections.scenario: Kickoff call. Client states a specific headcount reduction and a specific quarter, before any scoping, testing, or accuracy benchmarking has happened on their actual data.
contentSections.question: Why is staying silent on this statement a real risk to the engagement, independent of how well the technology eventually performs?

options.label: An unaddressed expectation stated this early tends to become the standard the engagement gets judged against later, whether or not it was ever realistic
Clients are generally wrong about what AI can do, so their expectations should always be corrected
This isn't actually a risk — the technical work will speak for itself regardless of what was said in the kickoff

feedback.unaddressed-becomes-metric: Correct. Nothing about staying silent makes the statement go away — it sits there as the implicit success criterion the client will use to judge the engagement, whether or not anyone ever agreed it was realistic. Naming the gap early gives both sides a chance to set a criterion that's actually connected to what scoping and testing show is achievable.
feedback.client-is-always-wrong: The point isn't that the client's expectation is necessarily wrong — it might turn out to be achievable. The point is that nobody knows yet, at kickoff, before scoping, and treating an unverified guess as a confirmed plan is the actual problem, regardless of which direction it turns out to be wrong in.
feedback.not-actually-risk: Good technical work doesn't retroactively change what the client was told to expect at kickoff. If the stated headcount reduction doesn't happen on the stated timeline, the engagement reads as a failure by the client's own stated metric, even if the system performs well by every other measure.

contentSections.mechanism: In consulting engagements, whatever specific, measurable claim goes unchallenged early tends to become the implicit definition of success later, regardless of whether it was ever scoped or verified. Naming the gap between what's known and what's assumed, at the point it's said, is how a consultant prevents an unscoped guess from becoming the project's judgment criterion.

contentSections.body: Much of the actual value in AI consulting is catching and correcting expectation gaps before they harden into someone's success metric — not just doing good technical work. The uncomfortable correction in the kickoff room is cheaper than the failed-project narrative three months later.

title: '95% Accuracy' Isn't One Number — and the Difference Can Be the Whole Engagement
description: A single accuracy target hides two very different failure modes — missing a real risk versus flagging a safe case — and which one matters more depends entirely on what's actually at stake if the model is wrong.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish precision from recall as measures of a model's errors, not just its overall accuracy
Determine which error type (false positive or false negative) matters more given the real-world cost of each in a specific use case

contentSections.body: A client wants an AI system to flag risky clauses in legal contracts before a lawyer reviews them, and insists on "95% accuracy" as the success target, citing an industry benchmark. The process being automated is contract review, where missing a single liability clause can have real legal consequences for the client. "95% accuracy" sounds like a clear, reasonable bar — but it's actually hiding the one question that matters most for this specific use case.

"Accuracy" as a single number blends together two genuinely different kinds of mistakes a model can make:

- **False negatives**: the model misses something real — here, a risky clause that actually exists in the contract and doesn't get flagged.
- **False positives**: the model flags something that isn't actually a problem — a clause gets marked risky when a lawyer would judge it fine.

A model can hit 95% overall accuracy by being excellent at avoiding false positives while still missing a meaningful share of real risks, or the reverse — flagging everything remotely questionable and burying the lawyer in noise while still technically clearing 95% because most clauses in a typical contract are unremarkable. The two error profiles produce the identical headline number and are not remotely equivalent in a liability-sensitive process.

The consulting judgment call is: **which error is more expensive here?** In contract review, missing a real risk (false negative) usually costs far more than over-flagging a safe clause (false positive) — a lawyer re-reading one extra paragraph is cheap; an unflagged liability clause reaching a signed contract is not. That means the target shouldn't be "95% accuracy" in the abstract — it should be a recall target (catch nearly everything real) even if it costs some precision (more false alarms for the lawyer to dismiss).

contentSections.scenario:
The client originally set '95% accuracy' as the target for the contract-review model, before anyone broke that number down further. Two configurations were then tested against real contracts:

Configuration A: catches 99% of real risky clauses (recall), but also flags 15% of safe clauses as risky (lawyer reviews some unnecessary flags).
Configuration B: catches 85% of real risky clauses (recall), and only flags 3% of safe clauses as risky (fewer false alarms, but more real risks slip through unflagged).

Given that missing a real liability clause is far more costly than a lawyer dismissing an unnecessary flag: which facts below actually support recommending Configuration A over Configuration B?
contentSections.question: Select every piece of evidence that genuinely supports recommending Configuration A.

items.label: Configuration A catches 99% of real risky clauses versus 85% for Configuration B
In this use case, a lawyer dismissing an unnecessary flag costs far less than a real liability clause slipping through unflagged
The client originally pitched '95% accuracy' as the target for both configurations, before this precision/recall breakdown was run
Configuration A produces fewer false alarms than Configuration B

explanation.higher-recall: Applicable. Recall — the share of real risky clauses actually caught — is the metric that matters most given the cost asymmetry, and Configuration A's 99% substantially beats Configuration B's 85%.
explanation.asymmetric-cost: Applicable. This is the actual reasoning that should drive the recommendation: when a missed risk is far more expensive than a false alarm, the choice should favor whichever configuration catches more real risks, even at the cost of more false alarms.
explanation.same-headline-accuracy: Not applicable — that both configurations were pitched against the same 95% target is what made the headline number the client anchored on in the first place. It's evidence the original framing was too coarse to distinguish the two options, not evidence for choosing either one; the actual choice depends on the recall/precision breakdown, not on which one hits the original target number.
explanation.config-a-fewer-false-alarms: Not applicable, and backwards — Configuration A actually produces *more* false alarms than Configuration B (15% versus 3%). That's the real tradeoff being accepted, not a point in A's favor.

contentSections.synthesis: The right call is Configuration A, and the reasoning that gets there is recall plus cost asymmetry — not the shared headline accuracy number, and not false-alarm rate in isolation. A lawyer spending a few extra minutes dismissing an unnecessary flag is a minor cost; a real liability clause reaching a signed contract unflagged is a serious one. The consulting skill is identifying which error costs more in this specific process, then choosing the configuration that minimizes the expensive error — not defaulting to whichever option has the higher accuracy number or the lower false-alarm rate in isolation.

contentSections.body: "Accuracy" is not a single, sufficient success metric for a risk-sensitive process — it hides the tradeoff between missing real problems and raising false alarms. The consultant's job is surfacing that tradeoff explicitly and asking which error costs more given what's actually at stake, not accepting a client's single accuracy number at face value.
